notes: \cpara{Picks up the baseball example from the previous day's post, ``Taboo Your Words'' (15 February 2008), and states the goal: to describe a thing without its usual word, not to find a synonym the card happens to allow.}

\cpara{The answer: visualize, as in the earlier post ``Original Seeing'' (October 2007). That post quotes Robert Pirsig's story of a student who could write only after she was told to start with one brick of one building.}
\cpara{The first of three worked examples: the bat, described by its shape, material and use.}
\cpara{The second example: the ball.}
\cpara{The third example: the bases, described by their role in the game's rules.}
\cpara{Names the obstacle: a familiar word stands in for the details and hides them. Links the point to two earlier posts, on clich\'es and on cached thoughts.}
\cpara{Ranks Taboo among the ``fundamental'' capacities, on the same level as asking ``Why?'' The ranking is asserted; no reason is given for it.}
\cpara{Lists six related ideas, each with a one-clause reason: pragmatism, reductionism, hugging the query, avoiding cached thoughts, ``Show, don't tell!'', and keeping one's purpose.}
\cpara{Quotes the author's ``Lost Purposes'' (25 November 2007) word for word: a student studies ``12th-century knitting patterns'' only because the degree, and then the job, require it.}
\cpara{Applies the method to school, with a deliberately bleak picture of what one would notice, hedged with ``currently seems.''}
\cpara{Connects lost purposes to categories: anyone who attends college matches ``getting an education,'' whether or not they learn.}

\cpara{The post's new step: a mental category that only partly matches a goal can fail inside one head the way a proxy measure fails in an institution. The institutional half, teaching to the test, is Campbell's law; see the note on ``Lost Purposes.'' The step is illustrated by the one example of education and is not otherwise supported.}

\cpara{States the general principle: a category discards information, sometimes relevant information, and Taboo is the first remedy. The falling tree and the blegg come from earlier posts in the sequence.}
\cpara{Applies the point to the method's own name. The board game bans five words, which is not enough to force original seeing, so what matches the label ``play Taboo'' need not serve the purpose.}

\cpara{Specifies the method more fully than ``Taboo Your Words'' did. The player bans, by choice, the synonyms the card leaves out, and any newly coined word or phrase that would serve as the same handle.}
\cpara{Asks the reader to turn the method on the method: what is each part of playing Taboo for?}
\cpara{Generalizes: seeing one's activities afresh shows one's goals, and habits one would otherwise not keep.}
\cpara{Summarizes: purpose is lost when a symbol (a degree, a test score, medical care) displaces the substance (learning, knowledge, health), and the cure is the reverse.}
\cpara{The title's instruction, given in eleven phrasings in one sentence. The phrasings borrow terms from linguistics, programming and maps.}

\cpara{Points to a finished application of the method, ``The Simple Truth.'' That dialogue does describe reality in lower-level terms, as ``whatever-it-is that determines my experimental results.'' The parenthesis also gives a partial answer to the stopping question raised in the notes on ``Taboo Your Words'': the test is whether the result ``fulfilled its purpose.''}

\cfact{The published text of ``The Simple Truth'' uses several of the listed words: forms of ``believe'' and ``belief'' 54 times, ``reality'' 15 times, ``semantic'' once. They occur in the narrator's own account, not only in the opponents' lines: ``The correspondence between reality and my beliefs comes from reality controlling my beliefs, not the other way around.'' The parenthesis that follows names only ``true'' as an exception.}
\cpara{A second example: Bayes's rule states what evidence does in mathematics. The claim that trying to define such terms in words means you ``just go in circles'' is given without argument.}

\cpara{The word is not named; the posts linked here make it ``rational'' or ``rationality.'' The earlier warnings gave a reason close to this one. In ``Twelve Virtues of Rationality,'' telling yourself ``It is my duty to be rational'' is said to ``only enshrine your mistaken conception.''}
